chapter: Kansas City rooms and Piney Brown
title: Piney Brown's policy wheels and Little Piney
summary: Goodwin says Piney's money came from policy wheels, backed by Felix Payne, and distinguishes Big Piney from Little Piney.

story.theme_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and rough clubs of Prohibition
story.community_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and the Prohibition-era clubs

blocks.x: That was the equalizer. Crook, tell me, where did Piney get his money? I think most of us might know
but we'd like to hear it from a native Kansas Citian who played the music.

Piney was -- actually Piney operated the policy wheel. He had -- he made plenty of money. In fact, if I'm not mistaken, I think he had two or three policy wheels in town. Him and another fellow -- this was a white fellow by the name of Bud Smith I believe it was -- they both operated the bigtime policy wheel thing in town and this was -- this was where Piney got money and it was another fellow here by the name of Felix Payne who also backed Piney in his policy venture.

Felix Payne was a top -- one of the top gamblers in town and there was another fellow by the name of Little Piney. There was a Big Piney and a Little Piney. They both were gamblers and but when Big Piney was the last of the bigtime spenders. He would -- Piney would always furnish the money.
Well, let me ask this Crook. When they talk about Piney Brown, I would guess they were talking about Big Piney?
